text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Conservative Party MPs plan to oppose a government plan to restrict the sale of old state-subsidised blocks of flats currently leased in the Arava-system.
- Police start week-long national campaign to stop small speeding violations since many drivers constantly exceed speed limist by some 10 kilometres per hour. @

- Joensuu is Finland's most expensive city, Tampere the cheapest in terms of an average family's cost of living including taxes and other fees, study by the taxpayers' lobby and City of Helsinki shows.
- Big pension insurers boosted their investment income clearly last year.
- Finland will not give up its seat on the EU commission, says Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen on official visit to Germany.
- Seventy-four percent of Finns would be prepared to work shorter hours, even it meant lost income, to ease the unemployment situation, Suomen Gallup poll shows. @
- Finns watched telvision 10 minutes more per day last year than a year earlier, 2 hours 41 minutes for the over 10-year-old population. Sports and poor weather boosted TV audiences.
- Ministry of social affairs could not reach conclusion on Wednesday on planned change in interest rate of pension funds' credits to companies (TEL); next chance will be on Friday.
- Over-production has lowered oil prices significantly but gasoline and fuel oil prices are not expected to fall markedly, industry says. @
- Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen condemns the appointment of Bank board member Harri Holkeri as national carrier Finnair's non-executive chairman.

- European Commission's approval of Kesko's plans to sell most of Tuko may come in time before Kesko's agreements with buyers expire at the end of April. The commission has received the trustee's report and must reply within 14 days. @
KAUPPALEHTI

- Government has changed policy on how to use privatisation proceeds, initially due to be earmarked to develop industry. At least one billion of some 2.5 billion of proceeds will be used for general expenditure -- reducing borrowing -- and R&D spending will rise to 1.5 billion, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto says.

- The number of petrol stations will fall and market will become polarised with unmanned taps on one hand and full-service stations on the other, report by the Helsinki Centre for Business Studies says. @
AAMULEHTI
- Cooperative bank director Reijo Karhinen says Finnish banks may still by the start of next decade halve the number of branches from 1,700.
- Finance ministry is planning to cut support for house construction since the sector is recovering so rapidly.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Union of municipal employees (KTV) threatens strike in Turku unless the city makes a deal with staff of its telephone operator to secure their position if the company is privatised as is planned. @
- Tough competition for cargo has started in shipping to and from southeastern Finland, with Finnlink challenging Silja Line, Viking Line and Seawind Line.
DEMARI
- Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK) proposes shorter working hours as part of next incomes settlement. The Confederation of Industry and Employers (TT) sharply rejects the idea. @
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Nicotine addiction is in the same class as heroin and cocaine addiction, expert researcher says.
- Rock concerts in Helsinki are few but large; small upcoming bands still prefer Stockholm, says Juhani Merimaa, managing director of Helsinki's Tavastia rock-club.
